title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass — Learning to Read
author: Frederick Douglass
text: Very soon after I went to live with Mr. and Mrs. Auld, she very kindly commenced to teach me the A, B, C. After I had learned this, she assisted me in learning to spell words of three or four letters. Just at this point of my progress, Mr. Auld found out what was going on, and at once forbade Mrs. Auld to instruct me further, telling her, among other things, that it was unlawful, as well as unsafe, to teach a slave to read. To use his own words, further, he said, "If you give a nigger an inch, he will take an ell. A nigger should know nothing but to obey his master—to do as he is told to do. Learning would spoil the best nigger in the world. Now," said he, "if you teach that nigger (speaking of myself) how to read, there would be no keeping him. It would forever unfit him to be a slave. He would at once become unmanageable, and of no value to his master. As to himself, it could do him no good, but a great deal of harm. It would make him discontented and unhappy." These words sank deep into my heart, stirred up sentiments within that lay slumbering, and called into existence an entirely new train of thought. It was a new and special revelation, explaining dark and mysterious things, with which my youthful understanding had struggled, but struggled in vain. I now understood what had been to me a most perplexing difficulty—to wit, the white man's power to enslave the black man. It was a grand achievement, and I prized it highly. From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, first edition, The Anti-Slavery Office, Boston, 1845
selection_notes: Chapter VI. This passage presents one of the most significant moments in the Narrative: the episode in which Douglass overhears Mr. Auld's prohibition against teaching slaves to read and realizes that literacy is the pathway from slavery to freedom. The extract contains three structural elements essential for analysis: (1) the narrated event (Mrs. Auld's initial instruction and Mr. Auld's prohibition), (2) the direct quotation of the slaveholder's rationale (preserving the racial slur and the logic of enforced ignorance), and (3) Douglass's interpretive response (the 'new and special revelation' that literacy equals liberation). The passage preserves the autobiographical narrative frame, the argumentative structure of the slaveholder's position, and the causal link between literacy and freedom.
normalization_notes: Original 1845 spelling and punctuation preserved, including 'forbade', 'shewed', 'to wit'. The racial slur 'nigger' is preserved exactly as it appears in the original text; it is essential to the semantic content of the passage and the slaveholder's quoted speech. The em-dash conventions follow the original edition. Quotation marks are standard double quotes; the original uses single and double quotes as was conventional in 1845 American printing.
